fields.expected: Most of what I've built comes back to retrieval and evaluation. In tSearch I built a talent-discovery pipeline that expands through public GitHub and Substack collaboration graphs, does identity resolution, heuristic scoring, and then rubric-driven LLM assessment, and the hardest part was never generating a judgment. It was finding the right evidence in the first place and being honest when the evidence wasn't there. I kept discovery and assessment separate for that reason. At Intelehealth I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard, which convinced me that generation is cheap and deciding what to trust is the actual problem. Search is the upstream version of that. If AI systems are only as good as what they can retrieve, then building the crawl infrastructure, embedding models, and vector retrieval that everything else depends on seems like the most leveraged place to work on it. I also want to be somewhere an intern owns a real piece of a system rather than isolated tickets, and Exa powering search for Cursor and 400,000 developers means the failure modes are concrete and testable.

fields.expected:
I built tSearch, a talent-discovery system based on the idea that someone's public work is a better signal of ability than where they went to school. It starts from named seed candidates and expands through public collaboration and publishing graphs like GitHub and Substack, then runs identity resolution, graph expansion, heuristic scoring, persistence, LLM assessment, and a recruiter digest. It's TypeScript and Node with Playwright, Express, Vite, and OpenAI.

The part I'm proudest of is the design constraints rather than the crawl itself. I kept discovery and assessment separate so the LLM judges can't silently paper over an identity-resolution mistake or re-run discovery, and I didn't collapse the heuristic discovery score into the LLM assessment score. I also made missing evidence produce "insufficient evidence" instead of a low score, because otherwise the system just re-ranks people by how much they happen to post. The judging is rubric-driven, with separate judges per dimension running in parallel and then synthesizing an evidence-cited assessment.

I built the MVP fast and later talked through product direction with Cory Levy of Z Fellows.

fields.expected:
I'm motivated by building systems around problems I actually run into, and then finding out whether they hold up. Job hunting is a good example. I got tired of repeating the same browser work across ATS pages, so I built a Playwright agent in TypeScript with SQLite as the single source of truth, because automation gets dangerous when application state diverges across processes. What kept me interested was not how much I could automate but where automation should stop. Free-text essays and demographic fields architecturally can never be auto-filled, and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags.

The other thing that drives me is retrieval and evaluation. At Intelehealth I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard, and that convinced me generating an answer is cheap while deciding whether to trust it is the hard part. Search sits right on that line, deciding what the right result actually is over the whole web. Working on crawling infrastructure, embedding models, and vector retrieval at Exa's scale is the kind of problem where the system either works for real users or it doesn't, and I want to be measured against that.
